title: Adaptive preemptive tenancy: latency-first yield with ephemeral KV leasing
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary: Implement an adaptive preemption policy that prioritizes latency SLOs by using ephemeral KV leases that enable cooperative, low-latency eviction and graceful yield across tenants in the continuous batching runtime. The design targets reducing tail latency regressions under GPU memory pressure while preserving fairness and avoiding abrupt token truncation.

Problem context: Continuous batching improves GPU utilization but increases contention for KV cache residency and GPU memory. Under pressure, hard preemption causes long-running requests to be dropped or truncated mid-token or to lose cached KV state, which increases latency and degrades quality for affected tenants. Existing approaches either (a) aggressively preempt causing high client-visible errors, or (b) avoid preemption and suffer high OOM/queueing.

Proposed approach: Ephemeral KV leasing + latency-first cooperative yield. Key ideas: (1) Issue time-bound soft leases for KV working sets per request or tenant group; leases include a small in-memory soft-reserve in the KV allocator and an associated lease token tracked in the scheduler. (2) When memory pressure is detected, the scheduler revokes leases by priority order (SLO-driven: low-latency sensitive requests preserved), but revocation is cooperative: the serving runtime receives a short reclaim window (e.g., 40-120ms) to persist hot KV entries to a compact spill format and update metadata rather than immediate eviction. (3) Lease extensions are granted heuristically based on short-term hit-rate and remaining sequence length; extensions are limited to prevent starvation. (4) A proportional temporal fairness layer ensures tenants receive time-slice weight proportional to committed contract tiers while benefiting from reclaimed caches when idle. (5) Integrate predictive KV eviction using a fast heatmap estimator (per-tenant short-window access frequency) to choose minimal eviction footprint required to meet memory headroom targets.

Mechanisms and components: scheduler lease manager, per-tenant lease table (ephemeral metadata only), cooperative reclaim API in runtime, predictive heatmap estimator, soft-admission control for long-running generation (token budget-aware admission), metrics for lease churn, lease extension rate, preemption latency, and SLO violation delta.

Trade-offs: Cooperative reclaim reduces quality loss but increases implementation complexity and slightly increases worst-case reclaim latency. Predictive eviction reduces churn but can be mispredicted for bursty patterns. Soft leases risk tenants holding memory longer than strictly optimal—mitigated by strict extension budgets and backstop urgent-reclaim that forces immediate eviction in critical OOM situations.

Rollout path: feature-flagged canary > host-only traffic with synthetic workload > internal Dedicated pool > gradual customer rollout with opt-in. Monitoring and automated rollback if p95 latency worsens by >10% or OOMs increase.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler exposes ephemeral KV lease API and runtime implements cooperative reclaim handshake.
Unit + integration tests validate lease issuance, extension limits, cooperative reclaim window behavior, and forced urgent-reclaim fallback.
Benchmark: under mixed bursty workload, p95 latency for latency-sensitive tenants does not regress by more than 5% and p99 improves over baseline with hard preemption.
Memory behavior: total KV churn (entries evicted and restored) decreases by >=20% in synthetic hotset scenarios vs current abrupt-evict baseline.
Canary rollout shows no increase in user-facing truncations; metrics track lease churn and extension rates and are wired into an alerting policy.
